outcomes.measure_name: Mean pointing error (median initial movement direction error per episode)
outcomes.higher_is_better_evidence: Their errors increased abruptly at the onset of the adaptation phase, and then gradually dropped again. Most importantly, adaptive improvement was more pronounced for young than for old subjects.
outcomes.operationalization: Angular error of the initial movement direction (between movement onset and peak velocity), median per 50-s episode per subject, at the end of the 15 adaptation episodes with +60° rotated visual feedback (i.e. episode 20 in Fig. 1, the last adaptation episode); the paper reports no block average for the adaptation phase.

sources.locator: Fig. 1, x-axis 'pointing episode', last adaptation episode (episode 20), filled triangles (young) and filled squares (old), with vertical error bars
sources.quote: Fig. 1 Mean pointing errors of young (triangles) and old (squares) subjects before, during, and after exposure to rotated visual feedback. Open symbols indicate episodes where visual feedback was absent. Also shown are the standard deviations
sources.error_bar_evidence: Also shown are the standard deviations
sources.notes: Only graphical source for group means of the adaptation phase; adaptation episodes are the filled symbols from episode 6 to episode 20.

sources.locator: Results, adaptation-phase paragraph, exponential fit equations for each age group
sources.quote: An exponential fit yielded y=9.92+53.51×exp(−x/5.89) for young subjects and y=29.51+29.91×exp(−x/5.13) for old subjects.
sources.notes: Fitted-model parameters for the adaptation time course; the additive constants (9.92 young, 29.51 old) are the fitted asymptotic pointing errors, i.e. a model-based index of late adaptation. No dispersion reported.

sources.locator: Results, ANOVA over the 15 adaptation episodes (between-factor Age, within-factor Episode)
sources.quote: significant effects were yielded for Age (F(1,22)=7.58, P<0.05), Episode (F(14,308)=41.14, P<0.001), and their interaction (F(14,308)=3.44, P<0.001)
sources.notes: Age effect spans the whole adaptation phase (all 15 episodes), not only the final episode.

sources.locator: Results, additional ANOVA comparing pointing errors in episodes 20 and 26
sources.quote: we compared the pointing errors in episodes 20 and 26 by an additional ANOVA; the effects of Age (F(1,22)=13.78, P<0.01) and Episode (F(1,22)=7.79, P<0.05) were significant but not their interaction
sources.notes: Includes episode 20, the last adaptation episode (episode 26 is the first refresh episode after the break), so this age effect partly indexes late adaptation.

outcomes.measure_name: Mean pointing error (median initial movement direction error per episode) with visual feedback absent
outcomes.operationalization: Angular error of the initial pointing direction during the five after-effect episodes of pointing without visual feedback that immediately followed the 15 adaptation episodes (episodes 21–25 in Fig. 1); errors are plotted as negative deviations relative to the +60° rotation. The paper reports no block average.

sources.locator: Fig. 1, open symbols after episode 20 (after-effect episodes 21–25); first after-effect episode (21) for young (open triangles) and old (open squares), with vertical error bars
sources.quote: Fig. 1 Mean pointing errors of young (triangles) and old (squares) subjects before, during, and after exposure to rotated visual feedback. Open symbols indicate episodes where visual feedback was absent. Also shown are the standard deviations
sources.error_bar_evidence: Also shown are the standard deviations
sources.notes: Only source of group after-effect values; no numeric after-effect values are printed anywhere in the text.

sources.locator: Results, ANOVA on the after-effect phase
sources.quote: ANOVA yielded significant effects for Episode (F(4,88)=66.84, P<0.001) and the interaction (F(4,88)=3.95, P<0.01)
sources.values_in_text: Episode F(4,88)=66.84, P<0.001; Age×Episode interaction F(4,88)=3.95, P<0.01
sources.notes: The main effect of Age for the after-effect phase is not reported numerically (described only verbally as age-independent); the reported interaction is the only numeric group-related statistic.

outcomes.measure_name: Tracking root mean square error between target and cursor (RMSE)
outcomes.higher_is_better_evidence: subjects were instructed to follow it with their hand as accurately as possible. We subsequently calculated the root mean square error between target and cursor (RMSE) for each episode and subject
outcomes.operationalization: RMSE per 50-s tracking episode (initial 0.5 s excluded) for the control subjects, who performed only ten baseline tracking episodes with veridical feedback and five tracking episodes with +60° rotated feedback; late adaptation = the last of those rotated tracking episodes (thin lines in Fig. 2, episode 15). No block average is reported.

sources.locator: Fig. 2, thin lines (control subjects), last rotated-feedback tracking episode plotted for controls (episode 15); young = triangles, old = squares
sources.quote: Fig. 2 Mean tracking errors of young (triangles) and old (squares) subjects before and during exposure to rotated visual feedback. Bold lines represent experimental subjects which adapted to the rotation in a pointing task before being transferred to tracking; thin lines represent control subjects not pre-adapted with pointing
sources.notes: Fig. 2 shows vertical error bars but neither caption nor Methods states what they represent, so the bar type is unknown. No numeric tracking RMSE values appear in the text for either group.

parsed.notes: Numbers relevant to the two protocol outcomes exist almost exclusively in the figures; the text prints no group means for pointing error, after-effect or tracking RMSE. Locations deliberately NOT listed as sources: (a) page 3 refresh-phase ANOVA ('significant effects of Age (F(1,22)=13.42, P<0.01) and Episode (F(2,44)=6.18, P<0.01)') — this is the second, post-break perturbation block (refresh episodes 26–28), excluded by the dataset rule to use the initial round of adaptation; (b) page 3 transfer ANOVA ('Only the effect of Procedure was significant (F(1,43)=144,09, P<0.001)') — computed on above-baseline error of the FIRST rotated tracking episode (episode 11 minus mean of episodes 6–10), i.e. early, not late, adaptation, and pooled across experimental and control samples; (c) page 4 pooled-sample values ('The magnitude of adaptation in this sample was 0.49±0.21, and the normalized trail-making score was 1.78±0.55') — these come from an enlarged sample of 54 seniors supplemented with two previous unpublished experiments, with no matching young-group value, so they do not describe dataset 1; (d) trail-making and psychomotor-speed means on pages 3–4 (27.4±7.2 s young vs 42.5±6.9 s old; 77.55±18.40 vs 103.93±16.26) — cognitive screening, not a protocol outcome. Direction for the aftereffect outcome was left 'unknown': the paper plots after-effects as signed negative angular errors and never states whether larger magnitude is better, discussing it only as an index of recalibration that may be inflated by perseveration. Moderator information for reference: task_type visuomotor rotation, perturbation 'visual feedback was rotated by +60° about the starting dot' (page 2), pointing task with 'visual targets appeared in one of eight possible directions around a starting dot, at a distance of 12 cm' (page 2).
